Question: A majority of the \(30\) students in Ms. Demeanor’s class bought pencils at the school bookstore. Each of these students bought the same number of pencils, and this number was greater than \(1.\) The cost of a pencil in cents was greater than the number of pencils each student bought, and the total cost of all the pencils was \(\$17.71.\) What was the cost of a pencil in cents?
Solution:
The equal purchases make the total cost a product of three integers. Using the usual whole-cent price convention, let \(n\) be the number of buyers, \(k\) the number of pencils each bought, and \(p\) the price of one pencil in cents. Then
\[
nkp=1771,
\qquad 16\le n\le30,
\qquad 1<k<p.
\]
The lower bound on \(n\) comes from having a majority of the \(30\) students.

Factor the total:
\[
1771=7\cdot11\cdot23.
\]
Since \(n\) divides this product, its prime factors must come from these three primes. Any product of two of them is at least \(7\cdot11=77>30\), so the only divisor between \(16\) and \(30\) is \(23\).

Thus \(kp=1771/23=77\). Its positive factor pairs, with the smaller factor first, are \((1,77)\) and \((7,11)\). The condition \(1<k<p\) leaves only \(k=7\) and \(p=11\). These give \(23\cdot7\cdot11=1771\), satisfying every condition. The price was \(\boxed{11}\) cents, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
